messages.subject: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.subject_clean: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.body_plain:
Good morning,
I am working on analysis of an aerial transect distance-sampling survey for moose in the Northwest Territories.  I was hoping to get some feedback on the approach I used to deal with different blind spots between aircraft to see if it makes sense or violates any model assumptions. The survey used two different aircraft, one was a Cessna 180 and the other was a Found Bush Hawk.  The Bush Hawk has bubble windows on all four doors which extend down almost to the floor.  When I plotted our detection distances by aircraft I found that the Bush Hawk didn't really have a blind spot under the plane, whereas the Cessna 180 seemed to have blind spot out to 150 m:

To address this I filtered out observations <150 m from the Cessna (FUGR).  I also filtered out observations >650 m for the Bush Hawk, and greater than 800 m for the Cessna.  This was to ensure that I was using observations from an equal strip width for each plane (650 m wide).  I then subtracted 150 m from the remaining Cessna observation detection distances.  This approach retained 139 of the 151 original moose observations.  It yielded the following adjusted histogram (each aircraft separately, and the combined histogram for both aircraft below it):

I then fit Half Normal and Hazard Rate models without adjustment terms to the data.  The fit of both models was pretty decent, but the Half Normal model performed slightly better based on AIC:
AIC -167.90
Distance sampling Cramer-von Mises test (unweighted)
Test statistic = 0.0445782 p-value = 0.908257
Abundance Estimate: 1804 (cv 0.17)
AIC -166.99
Distance sampling Cramer-von Mises test (unweighted)
Test statistic = 0.0481351 p-value = 0.887509
Abundance estimate: 1677 (cv 0.18)

I also tried models with left and right data truncation for both aircraft. Data was left truncated at 200 m and right truncated at 800 m, retaining 96 of the 151 moose observations.  The Half Normal model fit the truncated data well (CvM p-value = 0.96), but the abundance estimate was much higher (N=2977 and cv = 0.21).  The Hazard Rate model with the same truncation did not fit quite as well (CvM p-value  = 0.78) but yielded an estimate a bit closer to my approach outlined above (N = 1851 and cv = 0.2).

Any advice on which approach might be best to use would be much appreciated!

Thanks

messages.subject: Repeated Surveys for Pellet Based Distance sampling
messages.subject_clean: Repeated Surveys for Pellet Based Distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Good morning,
In one of our studies, we estimated white-tailed deer density at 3 study sites using distance sampling of fecal pellet piles, following methods in Urbanek et al. (2012).  At each site we searched along 600 m of transects.  We sighted few piles, so repeated the survey on the same transects weekly for 3 additional weeks.  At each survey we noted new piles, as well as which of the old piles had decayed.  In the analysis we treated the surveys as additional transect length, so 2400 m of transect rather than 600, and included each pile only once, regardless of whether it was re-spotted or decayed.  To convert pellet pile density (from program Distance) to deer density we used decay rates and defecation rate.
A reviewer of our manuscript noted that we should have recounted the re-sighted piles in our analyses, otherwise our estimate is an underestimate (since fewer new piles are deposited in a week than accumulate undecayed in a first census).
Any guidance or direction would be appreciated.
Thank you!
